newsitem.title: ITALY: OLYMPICS-ROME OLYMPIC FOES URGE IOC TO SEE THROUGH "FALSE" DATA.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-ROME OLYMPIC FOES URGE IOC TO SEE THROUGH "FALSE" DATA.

text.p: Opponents of Rome's candidature to host the 2004 Olympics said on Thursday that the IOC's positive assessment of the Italian capital's bid was based on "falsely construed data".

In an evaluation report on Thursday, the International Olympic Committee gave Rome and Athens positive assessments -- confirming them as front-runners -- but identified no clear favourite among the 11 cities bidding to host the Summer Games.

The IOC, which said Cape Town's bid was hampered by the South African city's rampant crime problem, said a short-list of five cities would be announced on March 7. The winner will be named on September 5.

"We're not surprised by this evaluation as it was based on superficial and falsely construed data provided by the bid's organising committee," said Cristiano Brughita, spokesman for the Committee Against the Olympics in Rome.
The Committee consists of hundreds of intellectuals and environmentalists who say the Games would be costly, disruptive and environmentally harmful to Rome, which last hosted the Olympics in 1960.
No one from the committee organising Rome's bid to host the Games was immediately available for comment. Promoters have promised that Rome would undergo a major facelift to be ready for the Olympics.
Brughita said his group, which has asked to meet IOC chief Juan Antonio Samaranch to discuss the matter, had sent a dossier to the IOC detailing "the falsehoods".

"In particular, we underscored the financial instability of the Rome bid and the uncertainty of promises made by the state since they were made by neither the government nor approved by parliament," Brughita told Reuters.
"The bid's budget is for 3.5 trillion lire ($2.08 billion) and would come entirely from the state or state-run companies or entities.

"We don't have that money right now and I'm not sure we'll have it in seven years," he said, adding that Italy was seeking to cut its budget deficit to meet the strict financial criteria to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
In its report, the IOC said Rome's notorious traffic could be a serious problem but added that it believed planning was being done to meet the transportation challenge.
Brughita said the IOC should think twice before believing vague promises to carry out major improvements in the Eternal City's transport system.

"In the proposal they sent to the IOC, they said it would take 13 minutes to go by car from Piazza Siena to Tor Vergata in the outskirts of Rome...I suppose they envision travel by helicopter," he said.

Piazza Siena, an equestrian complex in the central Villa Borghese, is about 20 kilometres (miles) from the Tor Vergata area south of Rome. It would normally take about half an hour to travel the distance by car.
